The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

derivations.claim: A polynomial $U$ is continuous and hence Borel measurable. Since $U\ge0$ and $\lambda\ge0$, [F4] gives $f(q):=\exp(-\lambda U(q))$ Borel with $0<f(q)\le1$. Thus $Z=\int f\,d\gamma_C$ is finite, and [F2] defines $\nu=f\,d\gamma_C$; [F3] gives its measure property. Its total mass is $\nu(\mathbb R^N)=Z$ by definition.

Under the displayed side condition $0<Z<\infty$, the scaled measure $\mu=Z^{-1}\nu$ is a Borel measure and has total mass $Z^{-1}\nu(\mathbb R^N)=1$, so it is a probability measure by [F3] and step 1.1. For a polynomial $P$ integrable under $\mu$, $\langle P\rangle_{C,U,\lambda}$ is then its well-defined integral by the notation in the Definition.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $N\ge1$ be finite and let $C$ be a real symmetric positive-semidefinite $N\times N$ matrix; positive-semidefinite means $u^{\mathsf T}Cu\ge0$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^N$. The centered multivariate normal Borel probability law with covariance $C$ is $\gamma_C:=N_N(0,C)$ as defined by [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]: every linear projection $q\mapsto u^{\mathsf T}q$ has scalar normal law $N(0,u^{\mathsf T}Cu)$, and the law exists even when $C$ is singular. Here $N(0,\sigma^2)$ is the law specified in [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]], with density $e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ for the standard case.

Let $U:\mathbb R^N\to[0,\infty)$ be a real homogeneous quartic polynomial, meaning $U$ is a polynomial and $U(sq)=s^4U(q)$ for all $s\in\mathbb R$ and $q\in\mathbb R^N$. For a coupling $\lambda\ge0$, define the partition integral and its weighted measure by

$$Z_{C,U}(\lambda):=\int_{\mathbb R^N}e^{-\lambda U(q)}\,d\gamma_C(q),\qquad \nu_{C,U,\lambda}(A):=\int_Ae^{-\lambda U(q)}\,d\gamma_C(q)$$

for Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R^N$. Whenever $0<Z_{C,U}(\lambda)<\infty$, the **finite Euclidean interacting measure** is the Borel probability measure

$$d\mu_{C,U,\lambda}(q):=Z_{C,U}(\lambda)^{-1}e^{-\lambda U(q)}\,d\gamma_C(q).$$

For a polynomial $P:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R$ with finite integral, write $\langle P\rangle_{C,U,\lambda}:=\int P\,d\mu_{C,U,\lambda}$. The exact supplier [[thm-qft-finite-euclidean-polynomial-measure]] proves that $Z_{C,U}(\lambda)$ is positive and finite and that every polynomial insertion is integrable. This is a Borel measure on finite-dimensional $\mathbb R^N$; it is not a measure on distributions on continuum Euclidean spacetime and does not by itself assert reflection positivity or reconstruction of a continuum field.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Let $k$ be a nonnegative integer, and suppose $\mathbb E|X|^k<\infty$, with $|X|^0=1$. Then $\varphi_X\in C^k(\mathbb R)$ and $$\varphi_X^{(j)}(t)=\mathbb E[(iX)^j e^{itX}],\qquad 0\le j\le k.$$ No converse is asserted.

Let $1\le p,q,r\le\infty$ satisfy

$$\frac1r=\frac1p+\frac1q,$$

with the convention $1/\infty=0$. If $f$ and $g$ lie in the corresponding
measurable-function spaces ($\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ or $L^\infty(\mu)$ according to
whether the exponent is finite or infinite), then $fg$ lies in the
corresponding space for $r$ and

$$\|fg\|_r\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

Let $I$ and $J$ be intervals, possibly open at finite or infinite singular ends, and let $\phi:I\to J$ be a monotone differentiable surjection. Assume $\phi'$ is locally Riemann integrable and the proper change-of-variable hypotheses hold on every compact truncation. If $f$ is locally Riemann integrable on $J$, then
$$\int_J f(x)\,dx\quad\text{and}\quad\int_I f(\phi(t))|\phi'(t)|\,dt$$
converge simultaneously and, when convergent, are equal. At several singular ends this assertion is applied separately to the corresponding ends; orientation is retained for decreasing parametrizations.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

derivations.claim: Let $Z\sim N(0,1)$. For an integer $k\ge0$, choose an integer $r$ with $2r\ge k$. On $|x|\ge1$, [F7] gives $e^{x^2/4}\ge (x^2/4)^r/r!$, so $|x|^ke^{-x^2/2}\le 4^rr!e^{-x^2/4}$. The right side is integrable by [F6], and the integrand is bounded on $[-1,1]$. Since [F2] represents any scalar $N(0,v)$ as $\sqrt v Z$ with $\sqrt v$ supplied by [F8], every scalar normal has finite absolute moments of every integer order, including the degenerate $v=0$ case.

For fixed $k\ge1$, define $T_k(u_1,\ldots,u_k):=\mathbb E\prod_{j=1}^k(u_j^{\mathsf T}Q)$. Each projection has a finite $k$th absolute moment by step 1.1 and [F1]. Applying [F5] successively shows the product is integrable. Linearity of each scalar projection and of the integral makes $T_k$ a symmetric $k$-linear form. The law exists under the stated Choice hypothesis [A1]. Since every polynomial is a finite linear combination of coordinate monomials, the triangle inequality also gives every polynomial a finite absolute moment.

On the diagonal, $T_k(u,\ldots,u)=\mathbb E[(u^{\mathsf T}Q)^k]$. Put $v=u^{\mathsf T}Cu\ge0$. By [F1], $u^{\mathsf T}Q\sim N(0,v)$, so [F3] gives its characteristic function $e^{-vt^2/2}$. At zero, [F4] gives $\varphi^{(k)}(0)=i^k\mathbb E[(u^{\mathsf T}Q)^k]$; extracting the $t^k$ coefficient of $e^{-vt^2/2}$ and dividing by $i^k$ yields zero for odd $k$, and for $k=2m$ gives $$T_{2m}(u,\ldots,u)=\frac{(2m)!}{2^m m!}v^m=(2m-1)!!\,(u^{\mathsf T}Cu)^m.$$ The identity also holds for $v=0$, when the projected law is the point mass at zero.

For even $k=2m$, define $W_{2m}(u_1,\ldots,u_{2m})$ by the pairing sum in the Statement; for odd $k$, define $W_k=0$. This is a symmetric $k$-linear form. On the diagonal, every pairing contributes $(u^{\mathsf T}Cu)^m$, and there are $(2m-1)!!$ pairings: pair index $1$ with one of $2m-1$ indices and repeat on the remaining $2m-2$. Hence $W_k(u,\ldots,u)=T_k(u,\ldots,u)$ by step 3.1, also for odd $k$.

For $k\ge1$, two symmetric $k$-linear forms agreeing on every diagonal agree everywhere. Indeed, for their difference $A$, expand $$\sum_{\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}^k}\left(\prod_{j=1}^k\varepsilon_j\right)A\!\left(\sum_i\varepsilon_i u_i,\ldots,\sum_i\varepsilon_i u_i\right).$$ In the multilinear expansion, the sum over signs cancels every term unless each label $1,\ldots,k$ occurs an odd number of times among the $k$ slots. Thus every surviving term uses each label once; symmetry makes all $k!$ such terms equal to $A(u_1,\ldots,u_k)$, and the sign sum is $2^k k!A(u_1,\ldots,u_k)$. Since the diagonal of $A=T_k-W_k$ vanishes by step 4.1, this sum is zero and $T_k=W_k$. For $k=0$, the empty product has expectation one and $\operatorname{Pair}(0)$ contains just the empty pairing, whose empty product is one, so the formula also holds.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. $$\mathbb E\!\left[\prod_{j=1}^{2m}u_j^{\mathsf T}Q\right]=\sum_{\pi\in\operatorname{Pair}(2m)}\prod_{\{a,b\}\in\pi}u_a^{\mathsf T}Cu_b,$$

where $\operatorname{Pair}(2m)$ is the finite set of partitions of $\{1,\ldots,2m\}$ into unordered two-element subsets. Thus every polynomial in $Q$ has a finite absolute moment, computed by finitely many covariance pairings.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$

$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

derivations.claim: Since $U(q)\ge0$ and $\lambda\ge0$, [F5] gives $0<\exp(-\lambda U(q))\le1$ for every $q$, so $Z(\lambda)\le1$. For each positive integer $n$, let $E_n=\{q:\exp(-\lambda U(q))\ge1/n\}$. These are Borel and their union is $\mathbb R^N$, because the integrand is strictly positive at every $q$. Since $\gamma_C$ is a probability measure, not all $E_n$ can have measure zero: otherwise countable subadditivity would give $\gamma_C(\mathbb R^N)=0$. Thus some $E_n$ has positive measure, and $Z(\lambda)\ge\gamma_C(E_n)/n>0$.

Fix $r\ge0$. For $s=0,1,\ldots,r$, [F6] and [F7] give the pointwise derivative $(-1)^sP(q)U(q)^s\exp(-\lambda U(q))$ and its next derivative $(-1)^{s+1}P(q)U(q)^{s+1}\exp(-\lambda U(q))$. If $\lambda_0>0$ and $|h|<\lambda_0/2$, [F8] bounds the difference quotient of the $s$th derivative by $|P(q)|U(q)^{s+1}\exp(-\lambda_0U(q)/2)$, since every intermediate parameter is at least $\lambda_0/2$ and [F5] makes the exponential increasing. Put $x=U(q)$. If $x=0$ the scalar factor is zero; if $x>0$, put $y=\lambda_0x/4$. The power-series estimate in [F5] at $2y$ gives $\exp(2y)\ge(2y)^{s+1}/(s+1)!$, so its reciprocal gives $x^{s+1}\exp(-\lambda_0x/2)\le(2/\lambda_0)^{s+1}(s+1)!.$ Thus these difference quotients are bounded by a finite constant times $|P(q)|$, integrable by [F2]. [F3] permits differentiation under the integral inductively through order $r$, giving $N_P^{(r)}(\lambda)=(-1)^r\int P U^r\exp(-\lambda U)\,d\gamma_C$ for $\lambda>0$. Taking $P=1$ gives the formula for $Z$.

The nonnegative Borel density $\exp(-\lambda U)/Z(\lambda)$ has integral one by the definition of $Z$ and step 1.1. By [F4], it defines a Borel probability measure $\mu_\lambda$. For any polynomial $P$, [F2] gives $\int|P|\,d\gamma_C<\infty$; since [F5] gives $\exp(-\lambda U)\le1$ and step 1.1 gives $Z(\lambda)>0$, $$\int|P|\,d\mu_\lambda\le Z(\lambda)^{-1}\int|P|\,d\gamma_C<\infty.$$

At $\lambda=0$, use right limits and right difference quotients. For $r=0$, dominated convergence [F3] with dominator $|P|$ and [F5] gives $N_P(\lambda)\to N_P(0)$ as $\lambda\downarrow0$; taking $P=1$ gives the same for $Z$. Now fix $r\ge1$. For each $s=0,1,\ldots,r-1$ and $h>0$, [F8] bounds the difference quotient of $(-1)^sP U^s\exp(-\lambda U)$ at zero by $|P|U^{s+1}$, since [F5] gives $0<\exp(-cU)\le1$ for $c\ge0$. This bound is integrable by [F2]. Dominated convergence [F3] inductively gives $N_{P,+}^{(r)}(0)=(-1)^r\int P U^r\,d\gamma_C$; applying [F3] to the formula in step 1.2 as $\lambda\downarrow0$ shows these derivatives converge continuously to their endpoint values. Taking $P=1$ gives the same assertions for $Z$.

itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $N\ge1$ be finite and let $C$ be a real symmetric positive-semidefinite $N\times N$ matrix; positive-semidefinite means $u^{\mathsf T}Cu\ge0$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^N$. The centered multivariate normal Borel probability law with covariance $C$ is $\gamma_C:=N_N(0,C)$ as defined by [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]: every linear projection $q\mapsto u^{\mathsf T}q$ has scalar normal law $N(0,u^{\mathsf T}Cu)$, and the law exists even when $C$ is singular. Here $N(0,\sigma^2)$ is the law specified in [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]], with density $e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ for the standard case.

$$Z_{C,U}(\lambda):=\int_{\mathbb R^N}e^{-\lambda U(q)}\,d\gamma_C(q),\qquad \nu_{C,U,\lambda}(A):=\int_Ae^{-\lambda U(q)}\,d\gamma_C(q)$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$
